title: Why They Scored an Own Goal—Then Defended Both Goals
description:
Barbados scored an own goal on purpose. Then they had to defend both goals.

In a 1994 Caribbean Cup qualifier against Grenada, winning by one goal would still eliminate Barbados. An unusual extra-time rule made a deliberate equalizer useful—and then changed what Grenada needed to do.

How did football's normal incentives end up reversed?

Sources:
Andrew Longmore — The Times, 1 February 1994, p.44: https://archive.org/download/NewsUK1994UKEnglish/Feb%2001%201994%2C%20The%20Times%2C%20%2364867%2C%20UK%20%28en%29.pdf
Kendall & Lenten — When sports rules go awry (2017), section 3.9.4: https://www.graham-kendall.com/papers/kl2017.pdf
RSSSF — Shell Caribbean Cup 1994 results: https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/shell-car94.html

Original illustrated reconstruction, not match footage. AI-generated narration.

#FootballHistory #CaribbeanCup #BarbadosGrenada
firstComment: Barbados weren't trying to lose. They were trying to qualify—and a one-goal win would eliminate them. The unusual extra-time winner counted double.
